title: Ang 975–983: Nat Narain
tomorrow: why would a hymn bless a woolen blanket?

cards: Some mistakes pile up quietly: a text not answered, a birthday missed, a promise half kept, until the pile feels too big to touch, so it doesn't get touched at all.
Ang 975 opens a new raga, Nat Narain, and Guru Ram Das starts right at the pile. Not with a lecture about how it got so big. With what happens to it.

teach.h: A SHORT RAGA, QUICK AND BRIGHT.
teach.b: Nat Narain is a short raga in the Granth, just these few pages, and musicians hear its mood as lively, quick and bright.

Guru Ram Das opens it, in paraphrase: O my mind, repeat the Name of the Lord, day and night; the countless wrongs you've done, the Lord takes them all and sets them aside. The picture is almost physical.
A heap of mistakes, and someone lifting it off you and putting it down nearby.
Not denied. Not pretended away. Set aside, so you can move.
So what does that give someone this week? When the pile gets big, the instinct is to freeze: I'm the worst, I can't fix all of it, so I'll fix none of it. Nat Narain answers with motion.
Turn toward the Name, and the weight comes off enough to take one step, then another.

Guru Arjan follows in the same raga, and the lively mood keeps going, hymn after hymn turning back to the same Lord. A bright, quick raga for a heavy feeling can look like a mismatch. Maybe that's the point.
A stuck mind doesn't need another heavy song. It needs something light enough to get its feet moving. Lively.

how: Ragis sing the hymns of Nat Narain, a short raga in the Granth, in kirtan; Guru Ram Das's opening hymn, on the countless wrongs set aside, is often explained in katha on repentance and a fresh start.

games.q: your little brother broke a neighbor's window and now hides from everyone, too ashamed to go say sorry. by Nat Narain, what helps most?
o: help him take one step: walk over together and say it plainly.
tell him it's no big deal; mistakes like that don't really matter.
let him wait until the shame fades, and go over then.
games.why: Guru Ram Das doesn't deny the wrongs; he sets them aside so the mind can move. the first step is the point.

practice: Pick one thing on your pile, just one. Name what you'd wish for it, what's in the way, and one small step you could take in the next day. Then let the rest of the pile sit beside you for the sit, set aside, not forgotten.
If you'd like, read ang 975 first.
